newsitem.title: BURMA: Burma maintains curfew in Mandalay as rumours fly.
newsitem.headline: Burma maintains curfew in Mandalay as rumours fly.

text.p: The military government maintained a curfew and other restrictions in Burma's country's second city of Mandalay on Friday following recent unrest, diplomats and residents said.

Rangoon-based diplomats said they had heard a young Buddhist monk had died after troops fired over the heads of demonstrating monks on Monday and that a mosque may have been burnt by arsonists on Wednesday.
Government spokesmen were not available for comment.

"We heard from our sources that a young monk died after troops opened fire over the heads of demonstrating monks in Mandalay on Monday," said a diplomat. "There was also a report that another mosque had been burnt on Wednesday."
Another diplomat said there were many confusing reports coming from Mandalay, including the death of the young monk.

The restrictions in Mandalay were imposed by the government after weekend clashes between Buddhist monks and Moslems when a young Buddhist girl was molested by a Moslem, government spokesman and diplomats said.
Residents in Mandalay said the 8 p.m. to 4 a.m. curfew slapped on several Mandalay townships earlier this week was still in force.

Soldiers set up barricades on several major streets and near temples, residents said. The military government imposed Section 144 of the Criminal Procedure Code, which bans gatherings of more than five people.
One Mandalay resident reached by telephone said rumours were rife "but nobody can verify them".
Diplomats said this week that at least two mosques were destroyed and several people were wounded over the weekend.
Residents said four mosques had been ransacked and at least two monks injured when security forces tried to disperse the monks from inside one of the mosques.

A statement received in Bangkok from the All Burma Young Monks' Union -- an offshoot of an exiled Burmese student's group based on the Thai-Burma border -- said the military had begun arresting monks, although no numbers were available.

"Fifteen of the detained monks have already been given summary trials and sentenced to lengthy jail terms. Other detainees are still being tried or awaiting trial in prison," it said, quoting information received from sources in Mandalay.
Official comment on the reported arrests was not available.
Burma is about 90 percent Buddhist and many of the country's monks live in Mandalay.
Monks played a key role in pro-democracy uprisings from 1988-1990 and many were arrested after refusing to perform religious services for soldiers and their families.
